Where it began

Yuvraj Singh was born on 12 December 1981 in Chandigarh, the son of Yograj Singh, the former India cricketer and actor. As a boy his favourite sports were tennis and roller skating, and he won the national Under-14 roller-skating title. His father steered him firmly towards cricket and took him to practice every day. He even found time for two small roles as a child actor.

He was playing for Punjab's Under-16 side at 13 years and 11 months. In the 1999 Cooch Behar Trophy final he made 358 against Bihar, who had been bowled out for 357, and at the 2000 Under-19 World Cup, which India won, he was Player of the Tournament.

The player

He played 40 Tests for India between 2003 and 2012, making 1,900 runs at 33.93 with three hundreds and 11 fifties, and holding 31 catches. His debut came at his home ground of Mohali in October 2003. His first Test hundred, 112 from 129 balls, came at Lahore in 2004, and his best, 169 against Pakistan at Bangalore in 2007, came during a stand of 300 with Sourav Ganguly. At Chennai in 2008 he made 85 not out alongside Sachin Tendulkar as India chased down a big target to beat England.

The wider world knows him best for the shorter game. At the 2007 World Twenty20 he hit six sixes in an over and reached fifty in 12 balls, and at the 2011 World Cup he made 362 runs, took 15 wickets and was Player of the Tournament as India won the cup.

What made him special

He struck the ball as cleanly as anyone of his time, and his punch through the covers was a thing to see. When he was going well the boundary ropes looked a little close. He was also a sharp fielder at point, with a strong arm and a good eye for the stumps.

Test cricket was the format where he had to wait his turn, in a strong Indian middle order, and he was a happier man against pace than against spin. Forty Tests across nine years still brought three hundreds and plenty of afternoons to remember.

Away from the middle

He received the Arjuna Award in 2012 and the Padma Shri in 2014. He married the British actress Hazel Keech in 2016. In 2014 he made a hundred for the Rest of the World XI at Lord's in the MCC bicentenary match, and in 2024 he captained the India Champions to the title in the first World Championship of Legends, beating Pakistan in the final.

And finally

Somewhere there is a national roller-skating medal with his name on it. Indian cricket can be grateful the skates went back in the cupboard.
